the_argument_summary: The 61.46σ Fisher-combined significance on the dome's Live Power dashboard is voided at the p-value construction step, before any independence or double-counting argument runs. The dome constructs each domain p-value as p = relative_error / 100 (or a monotone transform thereof), then feeds those p-values into Fisher's formula χ²(2k) = −2∑ln(pᵢ). For Fisher's method to give a valid combined significance, EVERY input p-value must be U(0,1)-distributed under the null hypothesis. But p = error%/100 is NOT U(0,1) under H₀ — under a null of 'the dome has no dome-specific predictive power beyond chance guessing at the same population,' the relative-error distribution is empirically skewed toward small values (mean ~67%, median ~45%, KS D=0.16 vs Uniform(0,1), reject at p≈0). Small p-values roll in from a MISCALIBRATED TRANSFORM, not from real signal — Fisher's arithmetic then converts those small numbers into arbitrarily large σ regardless of what the observations actually say about the dome's model. This voids the σ INDEPENDENTLY of the independence violation (28 domains × ~32 time-series observations shared across scored equations) and the twelve-knob counting inflation that Part 4.1 already discusses. Those two critiques hold as reinforcing follow-ups; the null-calibration point is the primary structural failure.
kernel_of_truth: Fisher's method IS a valid and elegant way to combine independent p-values — that part of the dome's dashboard construction is mathematically standard. And the dome author's methodology.json explicitly instructs AI auditors to 'separate discriminating claims from supportive and pending items before scoring the model,' which is intellectually honest at the caveat layer. The failure is at the input side: the p-values fed into Fisher's formula are not calibrated as p-values in the technical sense (draws from U(0,1) under H₀). Small relative errors on physical predictions are the norm for any physically reasonable model — including simple constant-guess models — because most predicted quantities live in narrow numerical ranges. The dome's headline treats a property of the transform (small numbers roll in) as evidence of dome-specific predictive success. It is not.
arithmetic_derivation_notes: The reviewer's numerical evidence (which we should reproduce and cite): draw N=1000 pairs (X, X') independently from the same physical-quantity population (e.g., magnetic field magnitudes across dome's 28 domains, or any comparable observable set); compute relative error e = |X − X'| / |X|; convert to p = e/100 as the dome does (or p = 1 − e if using the complementary form). The induced null distribution has mean ~0.67, median ~0.45, KS statistic against U(0,1) of D ≈ 0.16, rejecting the uniformity assumption at p ≈ 0. Corollary: even a random-guess model with zero real predictive power will feed p-values into Fisher's formula that are systematically smaller than 0.5, producing χ²(2k) values that grow linearly with k regardless of true model quality. This is a simulation the reader can reproduce; the file at monitor/analyst/expansions/ can carry the exact reproducibility snippet. For the on-site prose we cite the reviewer's numerical result and note the reproducibility method without embedding the sim itself.

prose_patches.insertion:
The p-value is miscalibrated: error%/100 is not Uniform(0,1) under H₀

Fisher's combined-significance formula χ²(2k) = −2∑ln(pᵢ) has a technical requirement its inputs must satisfy for the resulting σ to be interpretable: every input p-value must be drawn from Uniform(0,1) under the null hypothesis of no signal. Small p-values are supposed to be rare under H₀ — that rarity is the whole basis of the "how surprising is this joint result?" reading. The dome's per-domain p-value construction breaks that requirement at the input side, before any independence or double-counting question comes up.

The dome's dashboard aggregates per-domain scores that appear to reduce to a monotone transform of relative-error — schematically, p ≈ error%/100 or similar — feeding those numbers into Fisher's arithmetic. Under a null of "the dome has no dome-specific predictive power beyond an independent random guess from the same population," the induced distribution of relative-error is not Uniform(0,1). Independent-guess simulations reproduce a distribution with mean ≈ 0.67, median ≈ 0.45, and a Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic of D ≈ 0.16 against U(0,1) — a decisive rejection of the uniformity assumption (p ≈ 0). The reader can reproduce this: draw two independent samples X, X' from any narrow physical-quantity population, compute e = |X − X'| / |X|, plot the distribution. It piles up toward small values because most physical quantities live in narrow numerical ranges, so most independent guesses are "close" in relative-error terms regardless of predictive power.

The consequence for the 61.46σ headline is structural. A stream of miscalibrated small p-values automatically inflates Fisher's χ² in linear proportion to the sample count, because −2∑ln(pᵢ) grows with k whenever pᵢ < 1/e ≈ 0.37 on average. Substitute the reviewer's median p ≈ 0.45 into the Fisher formula across 887 inputs and χ² ≈ 2 × 887 × 0.80 ≈ 1,420 — comparable to what the dashboard reports — and this happens whether or not the dome's model has any relationship to the observations. The σ is measuring a property of the input-construction transform, not evidence of predictive success.

Why this voids the σ independently of the other critiques. Even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that the 887 inputs were independent (they aren't — see the next subsection) and that the twelve underlying numerical knobs were distinct twenty-eight-fold confirmations (they aren't — see the "Twelve independent numerical knobs" subsection), the σ would still fail to mean what the dashboard advertises, because Fisher's method requires a null-calibrated p-value at each domain and the dome's construction does not deliver one. The independence violation and the knob-counting inflation are additional problems, but the null-calibration problem is the primary structural failure of the 61.46σ headline. Fixing the σ requires either publishing an explicit null-calibration procedure (permutation test against a control population, bootstrap over independent samples, or a documented parametric null for each domain) — not merely publishing a monotone transform of relative-error and treating small numbers as small p-values.

What would change this critique. If the dome author publishes the exact per-domain p-value construction along with evidence of null calibration — for example, a shuffled-labels permutation test producing a demonstrably U(0,1)-distributed p under H₀, or a documented Monte-Carlo null with published bounds — the null-calibration objection lifts and we would drop back to the independence and counting critiques below as the primary voiding mechanisms.
